endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: The pilot exposed significant variation in rapid response team (RRT) staffing, training standards, and documentation practices across hospitals, making clear that a standardized operational infrastructure had to be built before expansion.

commentary.bottom_line: No study supplied tests whether standardizing response team staffing and documentation across sites before expanding an AI early warning system improves alert effectiveness or model performance. The recommendation rests on one governance framework that describes a pilot in which variation in rapid response team staffing, training, and documentation led planners to build standard operations before expansion.

perspectives.view: The evidence base contains zero studies that test the practice and zero studies that document the hazard. The only support is a framework description of a single pilot, which counts as expert opinion under GRADE. Certainty about the effect of cross-site standardization on patient outcomes or model performance cannot be rated.

The CHAI playbook reports that one pilot found variation in rapid response team staffing, training standards, and documentation across hospitals. The source does not report the cost, staffing hours, or time needed to standardize these processes. Leaders planning expansion have no measured estimate of the effort involved or of the benefit it returns.

commentary.research_gap: Multisite studies are needed that compare early warning system performance, response times, and patient outcomes at sites with and without standardized response team staffing and documentation. These studies should also measure the cost and time of standardization and test whether documentation variation biases model inputs or outcome labels.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested this practice, so no evidence covers Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Safety-net hospitals may have different rapid response staffing levels than the pilot sites, and it remains unknown whether a standard built at better-resourced sites would be feasible or effective for them.
